Page 95 of 127 DE-EE0009681 University of Maryland, College Park Figure 94: HP-TES model validation using field test data To demonstrate the HP-TES load-shifting capability, the validated model was used by varying the required control inputs. On the component level, the check valves associated with base HP, discharge, and recharge modes were opened and closed as necessary. The compressor input for on and off was also time-based, using the field-test data power requirements as the input. A time-based control was used for this simulated demonstration, with recharge hours set to 2 – 5 AM and discharge hours to 4 – 6 PM. At the beginning of the day, it is assumed that the PCM is fully discharged and has an initial temperature of 28°C. Figure 95 shows that for the simulated day, the peak power demand reduction ranges from 23% to 32%, with recharge power requirements 3 – 6% below the peak-hour power requirement. To improve the performance of the HP-TES during peak and recharge hours, it is important to consider reducing the hydronic loop pressure drops, and selecting pumps that are optimally sized for that secondary loop. Figure 95: HP-TES simulated field test day However, there are key differences between the simulated model and the system that was installed at the field test location. Firstly, the model utilizes water as the secondary hydronic loop heat transfer fluid, while the installed system used a 30% propylene glycol solution. Glycol solutions tend to have slightly lower specific heat capacities and thermal Page 96 of 127 DE-EE0009681 University of Maryland, College Park conductivities, requiring higher pumping power. Secondly, the simulated pump was based on that which was utilized for the laboratory-scale testing at ORNL as opposed to the field-tested installed pump, which could slightly alter the peak demand savings based on actual pump power consumption. Finally, the long piping lengths between the ground (TES location) and the roof (HP unit) were neglected in the HP-TES models, again changing the required pumping power. Nonetheless, given that the designed pump power ranged from 745 W to 800 W, the currently modelled pump power was tuned by adjusting the pump efficiency to around 780 W. Thus, it is expected that the peak demand reductions and recharge requirements will not change significantly. HP-TES Field Test Site Decommissioning The field test site was decommissioned and restored to its pre-installation settings. All components, pipes, thermal batteries, and supporting structures (ground leveling, fencing) were removed. The original 4-Ton RTU was reinstalled, and all necessary ductwork and wiring were restored.
